source_text: DE patientia locuturus, fratres dilectissimi, et utilitates ejus et commoda praedicaturus, unde potius incipiam quam quod nunc quoque ad audientiam vestram patientiam video esse necessariam, ut nec hoc ipsum quod auditis et discitis, sine patientia facere possitis. Tunc enim demum sermo et ratio salutaris efficaciter discitur, si patienter quod dicitur audiatur. Nec invenio, fratres dilectissimi, inter caeteras coelestis disciplinae vias quibus ad consequenda divinitus praemia spei ac fidei nostrae secta dirigitur, quid magis sit vel utilius ad vitam vel majus ad gloriam, quam ut qui praeceptis dominicis obsequio timoris ac devotionis innitimur, patientiam maxime tota observatione tueamur. Hanc se sectari philosophi quoque profitentur. Sed tam illic patientia falsa est, quam et falsa sapientia est. Unde enim vel sapiens esse vel patiens possit qui nec sapientiam nec patientiam Dei novit? quando ipse de his qui sibi sapere in mundo videntur moneat et dicat: Perdam sapientiam sapientium, et prudentiam prudentium reprobabo. Item beatus apostolus Paulus, plenus Spiritu sancto et vocandis formandisque Gentibus missus, contestetur et instruat dicens: Videte ne quis vos depraedetur per philosophiam et inanem fallaciam, secundum traditionem hominum, secundum elementa mundi, et non secundum Christum, quia in ipso habitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis. Et alio loco: Nemo se, inquit, decipiat. Si quis se putat sapientem esse in vobis, mundo huic stultus fiat, ut fiat sapiens. Sapientia enim mundi hujus stultitia est apud Deum. Scriptum est enim: Reprehendam sapientes in astutia ipsorum. Et iterum: Cognovit Dominus cogitationes sapientium, quia sunt stultae. Quare, si sapientia illic vera non est, esse non potest et vera patientia. Nam si sapiens ille est qui est humilis et mitis, philosophos autem nec humiles videmus esse nec mites, sed sibi multum placentes, et hoc ipso quod sibi placeant Deo displicentes, apparet illic veram non esse patientiam ubi sit insolens affectatae libertatis audacia et exerti ac seminudi pectoris inverecunda jactantia. Nos autem, fratres dilectissimi, qui philosophi non verbis sed factis sumus, nec vestitu sapientiam, sed veritate praeferimus, qui virtutum conscientiam magis quam jactantiam novimus, qui non loquimur magna sed vivimus, quasi servi et cultores Dei, patientiam quam magisteriis coelestibus discimus obsequiis spiritalibus praebeamus. Est enim nobis cum Deo virtus ista communis. Inde patientia incipit, inde claritas ejus et dignitas caput sumit. Origo et magnitudo patientiae Deo auctore procedit. Diligenda res homini quae Deo chara est: bonum quod amat majestas divina commendat. Si dominus nobis et pater Deus est, sectemur patientiam domini pariter et patris: quia et servos oportet esse obsequentes, et filios non decet esse degeneres. Qualis vero in Deo et quanta patientia, quod, in contumeliam suae majestatis et honoris instituta ab hominibus profana templa et terrena figmenta et sacra sacrilega patientissime sustinens, super bonos et malos aequaliter facit diem nasci et lumen solis oboriri, et cum imbribus terras rigat, nemo a beneficiis ejus excluditur quominus justis similiter et injustis indiscretas pluvias largiatur! Videmus inseparabili aequalitate patientiae nocentibus et innoxiis, religiosis et impiis, gratias agentibus et ingratis, Dei nutu tempora obsequi, elementa famulari, spirare ventos, fontes fluere, grandescere copias messium, fructus maturescere vinearum, exuberare pomis arbusta, nemora frondescere, prata florere. Et cum crebris immo continuis exacerbetur offensis Deus, indignationem suam temperat, et praestitutum semel retributionis diem patienter exspectat. Cumque habeat in potestate vindictam, mavult diu tenere patientiam, sustinens scilicet clementer et differens, ut, si fieri potest, multum malitia protracta aliquando mutetur, et homo in errorum et scelerum contagione volutatus vel sero ad Deum convertatur, ipso monente et dicente: Nolo mortem morientis, quantum ut revertatur et vivat. Et iterum: Revertimini ad me, dicit Dominus. Et iterum: Revertimini ad Dominum Deum vestrum, quoniam misericors et pius et patiens et multae miserationis, et qui sententiam flectat adversus malitias irrogatas. Quod item beatus apostolus Paulus commemorans et peccatorem ad poenitentiam revocans, proponit et dicit: An numquid opulentiam bonitatis ejus et sustinentiam et patientiam contemnis, ignorans quoniam patientia et bonitas Dei ad poenitentiam te adducit? Tu autem, secundum duritiam tuam et cor impoenitens, thesaurizas tibi iram in die irae et revelationis justi judicii Dei, qui reddet unicuique secundum opera sua. Justum judicium Dei dixit esse, quia serum est, quia diu multumque differtur, ut homini ad vitam longa Dei patientia consulatur. Tunc repraesentatur poena impio et peccatori, quando jam non potest poenitentia prodesse peccati.
pass_a_gloss: When about to speak on patience, most beloved brothers, and to preach its advantages, from what should I begin rather than the fact that even now I see patience to be necessary for your hearing, so that you may not be able to do even what you are hearing and learning without patience. For then at last a salutary sermon and reasoning is effectively learned if what is being said is patiently heard. I do not find, most beloved brothers, among other paths of heavenly discipline by which our sect is directed towards divinely promised rewards of hope and faith, what is more useful for life or greater for glory than that we, who lean on the Lord's precepts with obedience of fear and devotion, should especially guard patience with total observation. Philosophers also profess to follow this path. But just as false is their patience as their wisdom is false. For how can someone be wise or patient who does not know God's wisdom or patience? Since He Himself warns and says about those who seem wise in the world: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent. Similarly, the blessed apostle Paul, full of the Holy Spirit and sent to call and form the Gentiles, testifies and instructs, saying: See to it that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ, because in Him dwells all the fullness of divinity. And in another place: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks he is wise, let him become foolish in this world, so that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God. It is written: I will reprove the wise in their cunning. And again: The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are foolish. Therefore, if their wisdom is not true, neither can their patience be true. For if the wise person is humble and gentle, but we see that philosophers are neither humble nor gentle, but rather pleasing to themselves and, by this very fact, displeasing to God, it is clear that there is no true patience where there is audacity of pretended freedom and shameless boasting of an exerted and semi-naked heart. We, however, most beloved brothers, who are philosophers not in words but in deeds, and who prefer wisdom not in clothing but in truth, who know the conscience of virtues rather than boasting, who do not speak great things but live them, as servants and worshipers of God, offer patience, which we learn from heavenly teachings, through spiritual obedience. This virtue is common to us with God. From this, patience begins, from this its clarity and dignity take their origin. The origin and greatness of patience proceed from God as author. The thing to be loved by humans, which is dear to God, is commended by divine majesty: the good that He loves. If the Lord is our master and Father God, we should follow the patience of the Lord and Father alike, because it is fitting for servants to be obedient and for sons not to be degenerate. What kind of patience and how great is it in God, that, while patiently enduring the profane temples and earthly figments and sacrilegious rites instituted by humans in contempt of His majesty and honor, He makes the day rise and the sun's light shine equally over the good and the evil, and with rains, He waters the earth, so that no one is excluded from His benefits, and He lavishes indiscriminate rains on the just and the unjust alike! We see the inseparable equality of patience towards the harmful and the innocent, the religious and the impious, those giving thanks and the ungrateful, with God's nod, the times obey, the elements serve, the winds breathe, the fountains flow, the crops of the harvest grow, the fruits of the vineyards ripen, the trees abound with fruit, the groves grow leafy, and the meadows bloom. And although God is provoked by frequent, indeed continuous, offenses, He tempers His indignation and patiently waits for the predetermined day of retribution. And when He has vengeance in His power, He prefers to hold on to patience for a long time, sustaining and deferring, so that, if it can be, the malice, having been prolonged, may someday change, and the human, having been rolled around in the contagion of errors and crimes, may, even if late, be converted to God, with God Himself warning and saying: I do not wish the death of the dying, but that he may return and live. And again: Return to me, says the Lord. And again: Return to the Lord your God, for He is merciful and pious and patient and full of mercy, and He will turn away the sentence against the inflicted malice. Similarly, the blessed apostle Paul, recalling and calling the sinner to repentance, proposes and says: Or do you despise the riches of His goodness and tolerance and patience, ignoring that the patience and goodness of God lead you to repentance? But you, according to your hardness and impenitent heart, treasure up for yourself wrath on the day of wrath and the revelation of God's just judgment, who will render to each according to his works. He said that God's just judgment is because it is late, because it is deferred for a long time, so that human life may be consulted by God's long patience. Then the punishment is represented to the impious and the sinner, when already repentance can no longer be of use for sin.

pass_b_english: I am about to speak on patience, most beloved brothers, and to proclaim its advantages and benefits; but from what should I begin, other than the fact that even now I see patience to be necessary for your hearing, so that you cannot even do what you are hearing and learning without patience? For only then is a salutary sermon and reasoning effectively learned, if what is said is heard patiently. I find nothing among the other paths of heavenly discipline by which our sect is directed toward the divinely promised rewards of our hope and faith that is more useful for life or greater for glory than this: that we, who rely on the Lord’s precepts with the obedience of fear and devotion, should especially guard patience with total observance. Philosophers also profess to follow this virtue. But their patience is just as false as their wisdom is false. For how can anyone be wise or patient who does not know the wisdom or patience of God? Since He Himself warns and says concerning those who seem wise in the world: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent” (Isaiah 29:14; 1 Corinthians 1:19). Likewise, the blessed apostle Paul, full of the Holy Spirit and sent to call and form the Gentiles, testifies and instructs, saying: “See to it that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ, because in Him dwells all the fullness of divinity” (Colossians 2:8-9). And in another place: “Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become a fool, so that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God” (1 Corinthians 3:18-19). It is written: “I will reprove the wise in their cunning” (1 Corinthians 3:19). And again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are foolish” (Psalm 94:11). Therefore, if their wisdom is not true, their patience cannot be true either. For if the wise person is humble and gentle, yet we see that philosophers are neither humble nor gentle, but are rather pleasing to themselves and, by this very fact, displeasing to God, it is clear that there is no true patience where there is the audacity of pretended freedom and the shameless boasting of an exerted and semi-naked heart. We, however, most beloved brothers, are philosophers not in words but in deeds; we prefer wisdom not in clothing but in truth; we know the conscience of virtues rather than boasting; we do not speak great things but live them, as servants and worshipers of God. Therefore we offer the patience we learn from heavenly teachings through spiritual obedience. For this virtue is common to us with God. From Him patience begins; from Him its clarity and dignity take their origin. The origin and greatness of patience proceed from God as its author. A thing is to be loved by humans if it is dear to God; the good that divine majesty loves commends itself. If the Lord is our Master and God our Father, we should follow the patience of the Lord and of the Father alike, because it is fitting for servants to be obedient and for sons not to be degenerate. What kind of patience and how great it is in God, that He endures with the utmost patience the profane temples, earthly fabrications, and sacrilegious rites instituted by humans in contempt of His majesty and honor, and yet makes the day rise and the sun’s light shine equally on the good and the evil, and waters the earth with rains so that no one is excluded from His benefits, lavishing indiscriminate rains on the just and the unjust alike (Matthew 5:45)! We see the inseparable equality of patience toward the harmful and the innocent, the religious and the impious, those giving thanks and the ungrateful: by God’s nod the times obey, the elements serve, the winds breathe, the fountains flow, the harvest crops grow, the vineyard fruits ripen, the trees abound with fruit, the groves grow leafy, and the meadows bloom. And although God is provoked by frequent, indeed continuous, offenses, He tempers His indignation and patiently waits for the predetermined day of retribution. And though He has vengeance in His power, He prefers to hold on to patience for a long time, sustaining and deferring, so that, if it can be, the prolonged malice may someday change, and the human being, rolled around in the contagion of errors and crimes, may even late be converted to God, He Himself warning and saying: “I do not wish the death of the dying, but that he may return and live” (Ezekiel 18:23). And again: “Return to Me, says the Lord” (Zechariah 1:3). And again: “Return to the Lord your God, for He is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love, and He relents from sending calamity” (Joel 2:13). Similarly, the blessed apostle Paul, recalling this and calling the sinner to repentance, proposes and says: “Or do you despise the riches of His kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?” (Romans 2:4). “But you, by your hard and impenitent heart, are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works” (Romans 2:5-6). He said that God’s just judgment is just because it is late, because it is deferred for a long time, so that human life may be provided for by God’s long patience. Then punishment is presented to the impious and the sinner, when repentance can no longer be of use for sin.
